title: Breaking And Entering: Karen Marks
summary: Karen Marks joins Lauren on Breaking And Entering to discuss Karen’s former RRR show, the underground 80s music scene in Melbourne, and what to expect from her premiere show.
transcript:
Karen Marks joined Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studio on 23 March 2023, ahead of her Melbourne Town Hall concert on 28 April. They discussed the rediscovery of Cold Café, Melbourne’s punk scene, her work as a band manager and her long creative partnership with Ash Wednesday. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: It’s such a pleasure to have you joining us again in the Triple R studios.

Karen: Always a pleasure, Lauren.

Lauren: You were with us, with Simon and Michael Kucyk from Efficient Space, back in 2019, when the label released the complete collection of your works, Cold Café. I think we discussed at the time that you had a show on Triple R back in the day.

Karen: Oh, so long ago. Where was it? Cardigan Street, Carlton, I think, at the time. It was a midnight show. Ash used to come with me. I played very, very dirgy, depressing songs, which are my preference, of course.

Lauren: Do you remember what the show was called?

Karen: Music to Slash Your Wrists By, I believe.

Lauren: Your friendship with Ash Wednesday dates back all that way, and we’ll talk about it. You’re doing a one-off show at the Melbourne Town Hall, where people can hear your tracks live for the very first time. But first, that track we just heard: it was a reworking by a Japanese producer.

Karen: Well, so you told me. I’d never heard it before, and when it first went on, I thought it was me. I think it’s a bit of a case of spot the difference, because I really couldn’t spot much of a difference.

Lauren: I think that is definitely you singing.

Karen: Oh, it is. I don’t really know what they did to redo the song.

Lauren: It is quite similar. Listeners to Triple R in the ’80s would have known that single well. It was an underground hit, especially on Triple R, and it’s become a cult classic, recognised as one of Australia’s most popular minimal wave recordings. I played that Hotaru edit because it sounds like such a contemporary song. What’s it been like, from your perspective, seeing the path that ‘Cold Café’ has taken over the years?

Karen: Well, it’s fabulous, because it really didn’t do anything for many years. When we first released it, the minimal wave market, if you like, or the alternative market, which is what I called it at that time, was really, really small, too small, really, for it to make much of a mark. I think Triple R had just started. I don’t even know whether PBS was around. I know it was number one on Triple R and triple j at that stage, but it was a very small market. On reflection, I could easily have picked up and gone overseas, where the market was larger. I knew that really there wasn’t much for me here, musically.

It really just ran its course, and then nothing, really, for many, many, many years, until this new generation of record fans and collectors, and these new record companies, young, energetic people. The first I heard of it was from Michael Kucyk and his collaborators with the compilation album Sky Girl, which I think is terrific. I was contacted, looked into it and said yes, and was quite surprised when it came out on vinyl and CD and was released all over the world. Really, that was the start of this, and it did very, very well.

I think with the internet these days, it’s easy for a young artist to get their product around the world and to find their market if it doesn’t exist where you live. A lot of time’s gone by, but it got rereleased and hit a nerve, or a mark, where it fitted in with a lot of the things that are happening now. I’m thrilled about that. My support acts for the concert are fans of the song and of me, and that gives me a real kick. They’re young girls starting out, and it’s fabulous. I feel really, really fantastic about that.

The song really started because of Michael Kucyk finding it, and DJ Sundae and Julien Dechery in France. Then Michael asked me if he could put out the four songs I recorded at that time, which is when I spoke to you. Again, my followers are, I would say, largely overseas. But the market is huge now. It’s been a really fun journey. I say to Michael quite often, if it wasn’t for you, it would just be in a drawer, because I certainly wasn’t going to do anything with it. I’m very grateful for that, and I just think the whole thing is fabulous and fun, and a wonderful ride. It’s just got legs. It just keeps going, just keeps going. Then this idea of the concert was unexpected. Again, just another angle, another road to follow with the song. And here we are.

Lauren: Since we last had you on the show in 2019, there have been a number of these local reissues, and bands resurfacing from around that time. I’m thinking of Essendon Airport on Chapter Music.

Karen: They’re a cute little outfit. They’ve always been a really wonderful little outfit. I was sorry I missed that the other night. Did you go?

Lauren: I missed it too, unfortunately. They’re doing their first shows in a very long time, and it feels like there’s a resurgence of music from around that time. What do you think artists today are connecting with in that era specifically?

Karen: Well, I can’t really say. I just think music, in a way, is cyclical. You might get highly produced music for a while, and then people get sick of that, and then it goes back to being quite minimal. Really, let’s face it, there’s only X amount of chords. I believe that Ash was way ahead of his time here when we first recorded all of these songs. Now, of course, electronic music is a big, big, big market. There are festivals all over the world for electronic music, which I’d really, really like to pursue.

I think music always connects, really. It does go in cycles. We lucked out, hitting the mark when we came back when we did. Again, as I said before, the population has grown so much larger that the market is larger now. The internet means you’re not just relying on the market in Melbourne or the market in Australia. You’ve got the whole wide world.

Lauren: We’ve got minimal wave legend and icon Karen Marks joining us.

Karen: I love that, by the way. I’m using that.

Lauren: Go for it. Karen, I want to rewind. You’ve described the Melbourne music scene of your youth, in the ’70s and ’80s, as a big family who’d drive up and down Punt Road twice in one night, gig-hopping from the Kingston Hotel in Richmond to the Tiger Lounge, Martini’s in Carlton and the Crystal Ballroom. Could you take us back there and set the scene: what brought you to that moment, and your history in music?

Karen: Well, it’s quite a long story, so I’ll try and keep it short. It’s true that the rock and roll scene really was quite a small family, or really, we did feel like a great big family, and all sorts of music went. We’d go to these venues not really caring who was on, but everybody knew each other, and you’d know you’d meet up with your friends. All of a sudden these young men appeared in black clothes, and they were punks, and they came and started mixing with us and sussing out what was going on. Then a couple of the venue owners put the punks on, on a special night, and that was all starting.

To cut a long story short, I started managing The Boys Next Door, not for very long, just a short time. I was approached by this band called JAB, which was Ash, Johnny and Bohdan, who had come from Adelaide. I said, well, I can’t really, I’m already managing The Boys Next Door. But they kept at me, and then I stopped managing The Boys Next Door. That’s another story. Then I started managing them, and it became quite apparent that Ash and John were quite ambitious and quite serious about their music. It went from being a bit of fun to being, oh, we could really do something.

People were leaving the band, and other people were added. Pierre was added to JAB so that Ash could play synthesiser, and Pierre started playing bass. Then that evolved into Models, with Pierre, Ash and John. They auditioned people and got in Mark Ferrie, who knew Johnny from Peter Lillie’s band, and Sean Kelly, who Pierre knew from Teenage Radio Stars. There were quite a few people who auditioned, and then they decided on them, and that became Models.

It was Ash and John and I with the vision, I think, of where we wanted to go, and that we wanted to take it further. Then there were some, what do you call them, artistic differences. Models got really, really big, really fast. We would find venues and fill them to the rafters, full houses by nine at night. We had a huge following. We were Triple R’s darlings. We did all of their functions and live-to-airs, and it was huge, with Sean, Mark, Ash and John. I still think that was Models, really. Sadly, we never recorded. We were about to when the band fell apart. Ash and I decided to leave after a Sydney and Brisbane tour, because it wasn’t going the way we’d envisaged. Then Johnny left six months later.

But my relationship with Ash stayed. He was in a bit of a hiatus for a while. He had a studio in Brunswick Street, and we were really mucking around doing different musical things with his synthesisers and drum machines and things like that. That’s when we did this song. He ended up going over to Germany, thank goodness, where he was very, very, very successful, and ended up in, I can never pronounce it.

Lauren: Well, neither can I. I’m going to say Einstürzende Neubauten.

Karen: Einstürzende Neubauten, yes. I went to see them a few years back, when he came back, and I was just blown away. I thought they’d be a bit too avant-garde for me, but it was like art in motion. It was just extraordinary. Ash, because of medical reasons, ended up coming back to Australia a few years back now, and this is all happening. I wouldn’t be doing this without Ash, because I have no interest in doing music without him. We’ve just continued our musical journey together.

Lauren: It’s been a very important creative partnership for you, and a very long history. In his book Dig, Dave Nichols describes Ash Wednesday as a technical wizard who specialises in obtuse ideas blended with an incredible sense of melody. Is that your view of Ash as well?

Karen: Well, I wouldn’t have said melody, but I definitely would have said obtuse. He’s just brilliant, really. He’s just, as I said, ahead of his time, extraordinary, and very sensitive to other people’s music as well. He’s just a joy to work with. Anybody who’s worked with him finds him to be such a wonderful human being, and so clever, and so open to other people. I’m a big fan.

Lauren: Karen, I wanted to ask about the time you were managing bands like JAB and Models. You were one of very few female music managers then. I think you mentioned Caroline Coon?

Karen: Well, she was managing The Clash at the time, and I really don’t think there was anybody else. I know that female singers in the ’60s had women caretakers, if you like, or what do you call them? Chaperones. Some of my older musical friends could correct me if there was a female manager back then of the same ilk. But yes, that was problematic in a way when I was around. In another way, I found it incredibly easy.

I was interviewed once about all the problems and all the sexism, and really there wasn’t any, except once a guy asked me for a kiss when he gave me our fee at the end of the night, which I laughed off. Didn’t give him one, by the way. Apart from that, the boys protected me. I remember once there was a bit of a run-in backstage somewhere, and Johnny got very angry. I would have been working with John too, but sadly he passed away. I always think something’s three years ago and it’s about ten. I think it’s ten now; Ash could correct me. But we’ve never really gotten over that. He ended up back in Adelaide, and he passed away there.

As a manager, in the rock and roll music industry, which was full of men, only men, I think there was definitely a push to try and keep me out, which didn’t work. Definitely a push not to include me and not to give me any credit. It was, and still is, incredibly sexist. They say there are women in the industry, but they always do the picking-up-the-pieces jobs. There’s no one, really, who’s got the spotlight jobs.

Lauren: You’ve said that in your experience, punk was the first time women were allowed to play as well.

Karen: Well, yes. Helen Marcou invited me to speak at Why Punk, I think it was called, and the speaker before me, who I won’t name, said she found punk, all the boys, really sexist, and I just didn’t. I actually think punk was when women were able to pick up instruments and play with the boys. The Boys Next Door: I was their first manager. I was a woman. So I just don’t agree with that at all. I think the freedom that women then had musically, picking up guitars and singing and picking up bass guitars, it all really started then.

Lauren: It’s incredibly exciting that we now get to hear all of these songs live for the very first time.

Karen: And a couple more.

Lauren: I was going to ask about that. How did the Melbourne Town Hall show on April 28 come about? Did someone ask you to do it?

Karen: Miles Brown, who is the curator, or manager, if you like, of all the instruments for the Melbourne City Council, including the magnificent grand organ at the Melbourne Town Hall, is an artist in his own right, a conceptual artist and musician, and a huge fan of Ash’s, and a collaborator. Ash did an audiovisual show there with the organ, two or three years ago, I can’t say how many, and it was recorded. I think they’re just polishing up the recording of it. Miles turned out to be a fan of mine as well. Then there were just a few discussions about this and that, and whether we could do a show. I don’t have a film clip. Then the idea of doing a few European festivals came up, but we’d need some visuals, and then maybe doing a gig. Miles suggested the Melbourne Town Hall, and I thought, I can’t fill the Melbourne Town Hall. But apparently everyone seems to think I can, so I thought, all right then, sure.

The next stage: Ash and I had never performed this music with a band. That was always an interesting idea for us. So we said to Miles and Michael Kucyk that we’d go into Bakehouse Studios, get a rehearsal space with select musicians and see if it worked. If it worked, we’d say yes. If it didn’t, well, that’s that. We went in with Charlie Owen, Andrew Picouleau, Mal, I’m sorry, I don’t know his last name.

Lauren: Kilpatrick?

Karen: Yes, thank you. And Rick Hawkins, an old and dear friend of Ash’s and mine, who Ash has played with before. It was really, really fabulous fun, and it worked really well. So we said yes, and then we picked a date. The publicity department for the Melbourne City Council likes quite a long lead-up, so it was going to be February, but now it’s April the 28th. Sadly, Andrew Picouleau has got some health issues, so he’s been replaced by Adam Learner, who I know of, but don’t know. We’ve got a series of rehearsals coming up. But yes, the band has taken the music into a whole different ilk, if you like. I’m looking forward to it, and I hope everyone else is too. So far, the response has been wonderful. There will be a couple of extra songs.

Lauren: Can you tell us a bit about those?

Karen: No. They’re going to be a surprise. There’s one cover, and one of Ash’s songs added to the four.

Lauren: You’ve got incredible local support acts, too, as you mentioned: YL Hooi and Modal Melodies. I think YL Hooi are playing some brand new material as well. I can safely say both of those acts would be greatly honoured to be performing with you.

Karen: Michael, I think, and Miles were the ones who chose the support acts. I had another couple of ideas in my head, but they’d already decided they would be really complementary. Then it turned out that one of them is the daughter of a very close girlfriend of mine. That’s lovely. It’s really nice that she’s going to be supporting me, and it’ll be a fantastic night. I’m looking forward to it.

Lauren: You certainly paved the way for these artists and their sound. It’s going to be an incredible show, and very exciting to see Ash Wednesday playing the venue’s 1920s-era grand organ.

Karen: That will be featuring in the concert.

Lauren: The track we’re about to leave on is Ash Wednesday and, I believe, yourself as well: ‘Love By Numbers’.

Karen: Again, this is something we did with Ash in the downtime, and released. This is really more of an indication of Ash’s more obtuse persuasion. Thanks very much for having me, Lauren.

Lauren: I believe the record we’re about to hear from is a career retrospective of Ash’s that’s received the vinyl treatment, coming out just in time for these live shows.

Karen: Yes, there’s a compilation of all of his works that will be released in time, and it’ll be available to buy on the night, along with a few other surprises.
